tldr: This paper studies sensitivity enhancement in lossy atom interferometers using spin-squeezed states, focusing on practical metrology rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: Atom interferometers are limited by the standard quantum limit; spin squeezing can improve sensitivity but losses degrade performance. The authors aim to quantify realistic gains under lossy conditions.
method: A generalized input-output formalism is developed to model non-unitary interferometers with losses from velocity selectivity and scattering. One-axis twisted spin-squeezed states are evaluated for phase sensitivity.
result: Optimizing Bragg beam splitter parameters and squeezing degree can yield several dB improvement over the standard quantum limit despite losses, but finite temperature reduces the benefit.
conclusion: Quantum entanglement can enhance atom interferometry under realistic losses, but practical challenges like temperature must be addressed to realize the gains.

title: Symmetry-induced Logarithmic Relaxation In The Quantum Kicked Rotor
authors: Julien Hébraud, Floriane Arrouas, Bruno Peaudecerf, Juliette Billy, David Guéry-Odelin, Olivier Giraud, Bertrand Georgeot, Gabriel Lemarié And Christian Miniatura
abstract: We study the effect of discrete symmetries on coherent multiple scattering in the quantum kicked rotor. When the initial momentum is set to zero—as in recent Bose–Einstein condensate experiments—the effective pseudo-disorder becomes even under momentum inversion. The resulting discrete mirror symmetry of the dynamics profoundly alters spectral correlations: it generates quasi-degenerate Floquet doublets localised at opposite momenta, whose exponentially small splittings produce a hierarchy of exponentially large dynamical timescales. The coherent backscattering and forward-scattering peaks then exhibit a striking non-monotonic evolution and strongly asymmetric contrasts, followed by an exceptionally slow logarithmic relaxation toward a common asymptotic value—a hallmark of glassy dynamics, here emerging in a fully coherent quantum system. That such archetypal glass-like behaviour arises from a single discrete symmetry constraint reveals an unexpected and deep connection between quantum coherence and slow relaxation phenomena.
tldr: This paper shows that discrete mirror symmetry in the quantum kicked rotor leads to logarithmic relaxation, a glassy dynamics signature, in a fully coherent quantum system.
motivation: To understand how discrete symmetries affect coherent multiple scattering and spectral correlations in quantum systems, and to explore the emergence of slow relaxation without disorder.
method: The authors study the quantum kicked rotor with zero initial momentum, analyze Floquet quasienergies and eigenstates, and compute coherent backscattering and forward-scattering peaks analytically and numerically.
result: Mirror symmetry creates quasi-degenerate Floquet doublets with exponentially small splittings, leading to non-monotonic evolution and logarithmic relaxation of scattering peaks.
conclusion: A single discrete symmetry can produce glassy dynamics in a coherent quantum system, revealing a deep connection between symmetry and slow relaxation.

title: Optimizing Qubo On A Quantum Computer By Mimicking Imaginary Time Evolution
authors: Yahui Chai And Alice Di Tucci
abstract: We propose a hybrid quantum–classical algorithm for solving quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problems using an imaginary time evolution-mimicking circuit (ITEMC). The circuit parameters are optimized to mimic short-time ITE, using only single- and two-qubit expectation values. This significantly reduces the measurement overhead by avoiding full energy evaluation. By updating the initial state based on results from last step iteratively, the algorithm quickly converges to the low-energy solutions. With a pre-sorting step that optimizes quantum gate ordering based on QUBO coefficients, the convergence is further improved. Our classical simulations achieve approximation ratios above up to 150 qubits. Furthermore, the linear scaling of entanglement entropy with system size suggests that the circuit is challenging to simulate classically using tensor networks. We also demonstrate hardware runs on IBM’s device for 40, 60, and 80 qubits, and obtain solutions compatible with that from simulated annealing.
tldr: A hybrid quantum-classical algorithm for QUBO problems using imaginary time evolution mimicking circuits.
motivation: To solve combinatorial optimization problems on near-term quantum devices with reduced measurement overhead.
method: Optimizes circuit parameters to mimic short-time imaginary time evolution using only single- and two-qubit expectation values, with iterative state updates and pre-sorting of gate ordering.
result: Achieves approximation ratios above 0.9 for up to 150 qubits in simulation and demonstrates hardware runs on IBM devices for 40, 60, and 80 qubits.
conclusion: The algorithm converges quickly to low-energy solutions and shows linear scaling of entanglement entropy, suggesting classical hardness.

title: Qubit Operations Using A Modular Optical System Engineered With PyOpticL: A code-to-CAD Optical Layout Tool
authors: Jacob Myers, Christopher Caron, Nishat Helaly, Zhenyu Wei, Justin Oh, Zack Gotobed, Kotaro Yabe, And Robert J. Niffenegger
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2135 (2026).

Complex optical design is hindered by conventional piecewise setup, which prevents modularization and therefore abstraction of subsystems at the circuit level. This limits multiple fields that require complex optics systems, including quantum computing with atoms and trapped ions, because their optical systems are not scalable. We present an open-source Python library for optical layout (PyOpticL) which uses beam-path simulation and dynamic beam-path routing for quick and easy optical layout by placing optical elements along the beam path without a priori specification, enabling adaptive, path-based layouts with automatic routing and connectivity. We use PyOpticL to create modular `drop-in' optical baseplates for common optical subsystems used in atomic and molecular optics (AMO) experiments including laser sources, frequency and intensity modulation, and locking to an atomic reference for stabilization. We demonstrate this minimal working example of a dynamic full laser system for strontium trapped ions by using it for laser cooling, qubit state detection, and over 99% fidelity single-qubit gates with 3D printed baseplates. This enables a new paradigm of design abstraction layers for engineering optical systems leveraging modular baseplates, as they can be used for any wavelength in the system and enables scaling up the underlying optical systems for quantum computers. This new open-source hardware and software code-to-CAD library seeks to foster open-source collaborative hardware and systems design across numerous fields of research including AMO physics and quantum computing with neutral atoms and trapped ions.

.
tldr: Presents an open-source Python library for optical layout and demonstrates its use for building modular optical systems for trapped-ion quantum computing.
motivation: Complex optical design in quantum computing with atoms and trapped ions is hindered by non-modular, piecewise setups that limit scalability.
method: Develops PyOpticL, a Python library that uses beam-path simulation and dynamic routing to enable adaptive, path-based optical layouts without a priori specification.
result: Demonstrates modular baseplates for laser systems used in strontium trapped-ion experiments, achieving over 99% fidelity single-qubit gates.
conclusion: The code-to-CAD approach enables scalable, collaborative design of optical systems for quantum computing and AMO physics.

title: Bosonic Content Of Three-fermion Highest-spin States
authors: Jerzy Cioslowski, Krzysztof Strasburger, And Denis K. Sunko
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2121 (2026).

A rigorous characterization of the information content of any highest-spin three-fermion wave function is presented. It is based upon a formal decomposition of the wave function into a finite set of fixed invariants, called shapes, whose sole purpose is to satisfy the Pauli principle, and a variable part, constituting the bosonic excitations of these invariants, that provides its physical content. As an example, this decomposition is applied to a benchmark-quality approximate wave function of the lowest-energy quartet electronic state of the lithium atom. This wave function, which comprises hundreds of basis functions, is reduced to eleven shape blocks, only five of which are numerically significant. Such a compact characterization is a generic example of the appearance of superselection rules in configuration space, and provides a qualitative aid in the search for robust few-particle entangled states.

.
tldr: This paper decomposes three-fermion highest-spin wave functions into shape invariants and bosonic excitations, applied to the lithium atom.
motivation: To characterize the information content of fermionic wave functions and identify robust few-particle entangled states.
method: Formal decomposition of the wave function into fixed invariants (shapes) satisfying the Pauli principle and a variable bosonic part.
result: A benchmark lithium wave function with hundreds of basis functions is reduced to eleven shape blocks, five of which are numerically significant.
conclusion: The decomposition reveals superselection rules in configuration space and aids in finding robust entangled states.

title: Hidden Time-nonlocal Floquet Symmetries
authors: Sigmund Kohler And Jesús Casado-Pascual
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2112 (2026).

We investigate the Floquet spectrum of a detuned, driven two-level system and show that it exhibits exact quasienergy crossings when the detuning is an integer multiple of the energy quantum of the driving field. This behavior can be explained by a hidden time-nonlocal parity, which allows the Floquet modes to be classified as even or odd. Then a generic feature is the emergence of exact crossings between quasienergies of different parity. A constructive proof of the existence of the symmetry is based on a scalar recurrence relation. Moreover, we present a general scheme for its numerical computation, which can be applied to models beyond the two-level system. Analytical results are illustrated with numerical data.

.
tldr: The paper studies hidden time-nonlocal Floquet symmetries in driven two-level systems, explaining exact quasienergy crossings via a parity classification.
motivation: Understanding exact quasienergy crossings in Floquet systems is important for controlling quantum dynamics, but the paper focuses on a specific symmetry property rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: The authors use a scalar recurrence relation to construct a hidden time-nonlocal parity operator and numerically compute it for models beyond two-level systems.
result: Exact quasienergy crossings occur when detuning is an integer multiple of the driving quantum, and these crossings are protected by the hidden parity symmetry.
conclusion: The hidden symmetry provides a classification of Floquet modes and explains generic crossing features, but the work is primarily about Floquet theory and symmetry, not directly related to the user's research directions.

title: Anisotropic Fluorescence Signals Retarded Dipole-dipole Interactions In A Thermal Atomic Cloud
authors: Vyacheslav Shatokhin, Friedemann Landmesser, Mario Niebuhr, Frank Stienkemeier, Andreas Buchleitner And Lukas Bruder
abstract: We experimentally observe and theoretically explain anisotropic multiple quantum coherence signals in the fluorescence from dilute thermal potassium vapours, at room temperature and particle densities . We identify the retarded part of the geometrically fully resolved inter-atomic, resonant dipole-dipole interaction as the crucial ingredient to theoretically reproduce all qualitative features of the experimental spectra.
tldr: Experimental and theoretical study of anisotropic fluorescence signals from thermal atomic vapors due to retarded dipole-dipole interactions.
motivation: To understand the role of retarded dipole-dipole interactions in anisotropic multiple quantum coherence signals observed in fluorescence from thermal atomic clouds.
method: Experimental observation of fluorescence from dilute thermal potassium vapors combined with theoretical modeling incorporating geometrically resolved retarded dipole-dipole interactions.
result: The retarded part of the dipole-dipole interaction is essential to reproduce all qualitative features of the experimental spectra.
conclusion: Retarded dipole-dipole interactions significantly influence anisotropic fluorescence signals in thermal atomic ensembles, providing insight into inter-atomic interactions at room temperature.

title: Analytical Response Functions For A Compressible Thin Fluid Layer With Odd Viscosity *
authors: Yuto Hosaka And Shigeyuki Komura Abdallah Daddi-Moussa-Ider
abstract: Fluids composed of chiral active components can exhibit odd viscosity, a property that breaks time-reversal and parity symmetries. We investigate the hydrodynamic response to monopole and dipole singularities in a compressible thin fluid layer with odd viscosity, supported by a conventional lubrication layer. Using the two-dimensional Green’s function in Fourier space, we derive analytical solutions for the flow and pressure fields. These solutions provide a detailed description of the hydrodynamic interactions governing the motion of colloidal particles and microswimmers in confined chiral fluids, offering insight into the role of odd viscosity in modifying particle dynamics and collective behavior. The derived results are directly applicable to modeling transport, control, and self-organization phenomena in active and chiral microfluidic systems.
tldr: This paper studies hydrodynamic response functions in a compressible thin fluid layer with odd viscosity, focusing on chiral active fluids.
motivation: Odd viscosity arises in chiral active fluids and affects particle dynamics and collective behavior, motivating a need for analytical solutions to understand hydrodynamic interactions.
method: The authors use two-dimensional Green's functions in Fourier space to derive analytical expressions for flow and pressure fields induced by monopole and dipole singularities.
result: Analytical solutions for the flow and pressure fields are obtained, describing how odd viscosity modifies hydrodynamic interactions in confined chiral fluids.
conclusion: The results are applicable to modeling transport, control, and self-organization in active and chiral microfluidic systems.

title: Percolation With Coupled Lasers: Effect Of Non-linearities On The Phase Transition
authors: Simon Mahler, Nikita Stroev, Mahmoud Abu Rmilah, Asher Friesem And Nir Davidson
abstract: Controlled experimental studies of percolation are challenging due to difficulties in tuning site connectivity, isolating local interactions, and mitigating finite-size effects. In this work, we experimentally investigate percolation with a platform of coupled lasers, where connectivity, interaction strength, and system size can be controlled. Using a square array of lasers with astronomical number of possible cluster configurations, we show that the emergence of a percolating cluster corresponds to the onset of phase locking among the lasers. We also show that the percolation probability undergoes a second-order alike transition as a function of the site-occupation probability, with a threshold consistent with classical theoretical predictions. Surprisingly, we find that at low pump level, amplified mode competition (nonlinear regime) alters the effective behavior of the lasing sites and modify the nature of the percolation transition. The experimental results are interpreted by the means of a theoretical toy model with connectivity rules to the classical percolation.
tldr: This paper experimentally studies percolation using a coupled laser array, showing that the percolation transition corresponds to phase locking and that nonlinearities alter the transition.
motivation: Controlled experimental studies of percolation are challenging; the authors use a coupled laser platform to overcome difficulties in tuning connectivity and isolating interactions.
method: A square array of coupled lasers is used to realize percolation, with site-occupation probability controlled by pump level. The percolation probability and phase locking are measured.
result: The percolation probability undergoes a second-order-like transition consistent with classical percolation, but at low pump levels, nonlinear mode competition modifies the transition.
conclusion: The coupled laser platform enables controlled percolation experiments, and nonlinear effects can alter the percolation behavior.

title: Nonreciprocal Electrical Transport In Emerging Noncentrosymmetric Systems: From Hidden Symmetry To Functional Devices
authors: Shengyao Li, Zherui Yang, Xueyan Wang, Kian Ping Loh And X Renshaw Wang
abstract: Contrary to the reciprocal electrical transport constrained by the Onsager relations, nonreciprocal electrical transport arises in noncentrosymmetric systems where the resistance depends on the direction of current flow or external stimuli such as a magnetic field. Governed by symmetry-dependent charge dynamics, these responses appear as nonreciprocal charge transport (NCT) in the longitudinal direction and the nonlinear Hall effect (NLHE) in the transverse direction. Recent theoretical advances have expanded the range of mechanisms and material platforms capable of hosting nonreciprocal signals, revealing the role of hidden band-geometric properties. In parallel, experimental developments have exploited these effects for practical devices, offering promising alternatives to semiconductor-based rectifiers and wireless components, with advantages in broadband operation, ultrafast response, and high energy efficiency. In this review, we summarize electrical measurement techniques and characteristic transport signatures for identifying nonreciprocal phenomena and uncovering their underlying symmetry. We provide a comprehensive discussion of the fundamental mechanisms underlying NCT and NLHE, organized through representative material systems, and a subsequent examination of strategies for artificially inducing and enhancing nonreciprocity. Finally, we evaluate the technological perspectives of nonreciprocal electrical transport for electronic applications, along with key challenges and opportunities for scalable device implementation. By synthesizing current progress, this review aims to guide materials discovery and device innovation, and to inspire exploration of new symmetry settings and unconventional routes toward enhanced nonreciprocal functionalities.
tldr: A review of nonreciprocal electrical transport in noncentrosymmetric systems, focusing on symmetry-dependent charge dynamics and device applications.
motivation: To understand and harness nonreciprocal transport phenomena for novel electronic devices beyond conventional semiconductors.
method: Summarizes theoretical mechanisms (band-geometric properties) and experimental techniques for measuring nonreciprocal charge transport and nonlinear Hall effect.
result: Identifies key material platforms and strategies to induce/enhance nonreciprocity, with potential for broadband, ultrafast, energy-efficient rectifiers and wireless components.
conclusion: Nonreciprocal transport offers promising device functionalities but faces challenges in scalable implementation; further exploration of symmetry settings is needed.

title: Crystallography-driven Molecularization Of A Two-dimensional Spin- 3 / ...
authors: Hari Borutta, Tobias Müller, Ronny Thomale, Harald O Jeschke And Yasir Iqbal
abstract: Large-spin two-dimensional magnets are generally expected to develop conventional long-range order once the dominant exchange scale becomes appreciable. The layered spin- maple-leaf compound Na Mn O defies this expectation: despite sizable antiferromagnetic interactions and no evident disorder, it exhibits no magnetic ordering and displays two well-separated thermodynamic crossover scales. We show that this behavior originates from a crystallography-driven molecularization of the magnetic degrees of freedom. The low-symmetry structure partitions the Mn sublattice into inequivalent exchange pathways, generating a pronounced hierarchy that nearly isolates antiferromagnetic hexagons. Magnetic correlations therefore develop in two stages: first within individual hexagons at a scale set by the dominant exchange, and only at much lower temperatures do frustrated inter-hexagon couplings attempt to establish coherence across the lattice. While isolated hexagons reproduce the two-step thermodynamic structure, the experimentally relevant temperature scales emerge only once the hexagons are embedded in the frustrated two-dimensional network. The resulting quantum ground state is magnetically disordered, characterized by strong intra-hexagon correlations and rapidly decaying inter-hexagon correlations. These results identify crystallographic inequivalence as a materials-level mechanism for stabilizing molecularized and quantum-disordered states even in large-spin two-dimensional magnets.
tldr: This paper explains the absence of magnetic order in a large-spin 2D magnet via crystallography-driven molecularization into isolated antiferromagnetic hexagons.
motivation: To understand why the layered spin-3/2 compound Na₂Mn₃O₇ does not order magnetically despite strong antiferromagnetic interactions and no disorder.
method: The authors perform density functional theory (DFT) calculations to extract exchange couplings, then model the system using classical Monte Carlo and exact diagonalization on a frustrated honeycomb lattice with inequivalent bonds.
result: The low-symmetry crystal structure creates a hierarchy of exchange couplings that effectively isolates antiferromagnetic hexagons, leading to two-stage thermal crossover and a quantum-disordered ground state with short-range inter-hexagon correlations.
conclusion: Crystallographic inequivalence can stabilize molecularized, quantum-disordered states in large-spin 2D magnets, offering a new materials design principle.

title: Hybrid Monte Carlo For Fractional Quantum Hall States
authors: Ting-Tung Wang, Ha Quang Trung, Qianhui Xu, Min Long, Bo Yang And Zi Yang Meng
abstract: We develop a hybrid Monte Carlo (HMC) method to efficiently compute the physical observables from the samplings of the Laughlin and the Moore–Read (MR) wave functions of fractional quantum Hall (FQH) systems. With the advancements in methodology, including global updates and double stereographic projection on spherical geometry, our HMC simulation is significantly faster than the widely used Metropolis Monte Carlo scheme. As a result, we can readily simulate systems with electron numbers on both disk and sphere geometries. We apply this method to investigate the topological shift obtained from the edge dipole moment, computed from the wave function density on the disk. We also numerically computed the non-Abelian braiding matrices for different braiding schemes of the MR quasiholes on the sphere. Results with much better quality compared with previous works have been achieved. With the thermodynamic limit results obtained at ease, we also discuss the future usage of our method to clarify the questions on the instability of FQH states in an ideal Chern band setting or under quantum decoherence.
tldr: Develops a hybrid Monte Carlo method for simulating fractional quantum Hall wave functions, focusing on computational efficiency and topological properties.
motivation: Efficiently compute observables from Laughlin and Moore-Read wave functions for large systems, overcoming limitations of standard Metropolis Monte Carlo.
method: Uses hybrid Monte Carlo with global updates and double stereographic projection on spherical geometry to sample FQH wave functions.
result: Achieves significantly faster simulations, enabling computation of topological shift and non-Abelian braiding matrices with improved quality.
conclusion: The method facilitates thermodynamic limit studies and can address questions on FQH state stability in Chern bands or under decoherence.

title: Kovacs-like Memory Effect In Strain Stiffening Collagen Networks
authors: Maitri Mandal And Sayantan Majumdar Abhishek Ghadai
abstract: Materials driven far from equilibrium can encode memories of past deformations through long-lived structural reorganizations. Such memory effects-reflecting parameters such as deformation direction, magnitude, and duration have been widely explored in soft amorphous solids. Here, we report a Kovacs-like memory effect manifested as a non-monotonic stress relaxation in vitro biopolymer networks formed by type-I collagen, an essential component of the mammalian extracellular matrix. Using shear rheology combined with in-situ optical imaging, we find that this memory effect emerges exclusively in the nonlinear strain-stiffening regime, and persists over a much broader range of strain amplitudes than previously reported for other viscoelastic amorphous materials. Furthermore, we uncover a strong correlation between the memory response and the development of negative normal stresses and associated strain fields, highlighting the unique nonequilibrium mechanics underlying memory formation in biopolymer networks.
tldr: This paper reports a Kovacs-like memory effect in strain-stiffening collagen networks, focusing on non-equilibrium mechanics of biopolymer networks.
motivation: To understand memory effects in soft amorphous materials, specifically in biopolymer networks like collagen, which are important for biological tissues.
method: Shear rheology combined with in-situ optical imaging to measure stress relaxation and normal stresses in collagen networks under nonlinear strain-stiffening conditions.
result: A non-monotonic stress relaxation (Kovacs-like memory effect) is observed exclusively in the nonlinear strain-stiffening regime, correlated with negative normal stresses and strain fields.
conclusion: The memory effect in collagen networks arises from unique nonequilibrium mechanics distinct from other amorphous materials, with potential implications for biological tissue mechanics.

title: Continuous Thermochemical Sources Of AlF Molecules
authors: Pulkit Kukreja, Priyansh Agarwal, Maximilian Doppelbauer, Jionghao Cai, Xiangyue Liu, Eduardo Padilla, Sebastian Kray, Henrik Haak, Russell Thomas, Stefan Truppe, Boris G Sartakov, Gerard Meijer And Sid Wright
abstract: The AlF molecule, currently subject to laser cooling and trapping efforts, has the advantage that it can be efficiently produced in a thermochemical reaction between sublimated aluminum trifluoride and aluminum metal. Here we present a series of experiments with continuous molecular beam sources of AlF, utilizing this reaction. We demonstrate a compact AlF molecular beam oven whose total far-field brightness is molecules per steradian per second at 923 K, just below the melting temperature of aluminum metal. The continuous output from the oven begins to exceed the peak brightness of a jet-cooled, ablation-based supersonic AlF source for the , level, and we obtain an excellent signal-to-noise ratio with the oven in pulsed laser ionization spectroscopy experiments. By delivering flux from the oven into a cryogenic Ne buffer gas cell, we lower the rotational temperature of the beam to around 30 K and reduce its most probable forward velocity from 600 m s to 200 m s . In addition, we demonstrate that AlF can be made in a simple dispenser package, and observe that molecules thermalize to the laboratory temperature after colliding with vacuum chamber walls of the experiment. The resulting transient AlF vapor may enable direct loading of a molecular magneto-optical trap.
tldr: This paper presents experimental demonstrations of continuous thermochemical sources for producing AlF molecules, focusing on beam brightness and rotational cooling.
motivation: AlF molecules are promising for laser cooling and trapping, but efficient and continuous sources are needed for advanced experiments.
method: The authors use a thermochemical reaction between sublimated AlF3 and Al metal in a compact oven, and also test a dispenser package; they characterize the beam using spectroscopy and buffer-gas cooling.
result: The oven achieves a brightness of 10^12 molecules/sr/s at 923 K, outperforming ablation-based sources for the v=0, J=1 level; buffer-gas cooling reduces rotational temperature to ~30 K and forward velocity to 200 m/s.
conclusion: Continuous thermochemical sources of AlF are viable and can provide high flux with low rotational temperature, enabling future trapping experiments.

title: Distinguishing Near- Versus Off-critical Phase Behaviors Of Intrinsically Disordered Proteins
authors: Gaurav Mitra, Souradeep Ghosh, Kiersten M Ruff, Ruoyao Zhang, Gaurav Chauhan And Rohit V Pappu
abstract: Intrinsically disordered prion-like low complexity domains (PLCDs) drive phase transitions that underlie the biogenesis of many biomolecular condensates. Here, we report results from large-scale Monte Carlo simulations on lattices aided by computations of Binder cumulants and rigorous finite-size scaling. These approaches enable accurate mapping of the critical regime and computations of the full binodal of an archetypal PLCD. This weakly associating polymer undergoes phase separation coupled to percolation. Between the lowest temperature and the critical point, the concentrations along the left arm of the binodal vary by four orders of magnitude. The overlap line intersects the left arm of the binodal well below the critical point. This, taken together with the intersection of the percolation line and the left arm of the binodal, leads to demarcation of the binodal into three regimes. Regime I is farthest from the critical point. Here, the coexisting dilute phase is akin to a gas of dispersed polymers. The dilute arm of the binodal lies above the overlap line in Regimes II and III. Here, the semidilute nature of dilute phases enables clustering of polymers that is enhanced by intermolecular associations. The coexisting dense phases form confined percolated networks in Regimes I and II. In Regime III, which is closest to the critical point, the dense phase becomes unconfined and fragmented, and the system is defined by two interconnected, system-spanning networks. In addition to mapping the critical point accurately, we evaluated methods for identifying the theta temperature. We find that scaling approaches based on assumptions from two-parameter theories for homopolymers yield erroneous estimates of the theta temperature of an archetypal PLCD. Accurate estimation of the theta temperature requires direct calculation of the temperature dependence of the two-body interaction coefficient. We discuss implications for inferring solvent quality from scaling analysis of segmental distances of disordered proteins.
tldr: This paper uses Monte Carlo simulations and finite-size scaling to study phase behavior of intrinsically disordered proteins, focusing on criticality and binodal regimes.
motivation: Understanding phase transitions of prion-like low complexity domains is important for biomolecular condensate biogenesis, but the paper is purely biophysical without quantum or information-theoretic aspects.
method: Large-scale Monte Carlo simulations on lattices with Binder cumulants and finite-size scaling to map critical regime and compute binodals.
result: The binodal is divided into three regimes based on overlap and percolation lines; scaling approaches for theta temperature are shown to be inaccurate.
conclusion: Accurate estimation of theta temperature requires direct calculation of two-body interaction coefficient, with implications for solvent quality inference.

title: Electron Spin Drift In Long-distance Plasma Wakefield Acceleration
authors: Ming Zeng And Dazhang Li Yilan Guo
abstract: Plasma based wakefield acceleration of polarized electron beams has recently attracted considerable research interest. Previous works have found the forced spin oscillation of electrons due to two-dimensional betatron oscillation in particle trajectory and discovered longitudinal depolarization mechanism in plasma wakefield. In this work, we present a three-dimensional analytical model for the electron spin dynamics and derive the evolution of polarization during long-distance plasma wakefield acceleration. Our analysis reveals several phenomena including a transverse rotational spin drift leading to depolarization, a reversal of the drift frequency, and a consequent recovery of polarization. This work can offer guidance on future plasma-based accelerators for polarized electron beams.
tldr: This paper presents a three-dimensional analytical model for electron spin dynamics in plasma wakefield acceleration, focusing on spin drift and depolarization.
motivation: Polarized electron beams are important for high-energy physics, but spin dynamics in plasma accelerators are not well understood, especially over long distances.
method: The authors develop a 3D analytical model for spin evolution, incorporating betatron oscillations and wakefield effects, and derive equations for polarization dynamics.
result: They find a transverse rotational spin drift that causes depolarization, a reversal of drift frequency, and a subsequent recovery of polarization.
conclusion: The work provides guidance for designing plasma-based accelerators that preserve electron beam polarization.

abstract: Heteroepitaxy on nanocrystals of diverse crystal structures—hexagonal close-packed (hcp), body-centered cubic (bcc), and face-centered cubic (fcc)—is a powerful approach for engineering atomic arrangements. However, the mechanisms by which interfacial defects and strain relaxation accommodate structural mismatch remain poorly understood at the three-dimensional (3D) atomic scale. Here, we use atomic-resolution electron tomography to determine the 3D atomic structures and reveal heteroepitaxial mechanisms in Pt-based core–shell nanoparticles with diverse crystal structures including hcp/fcc Ru@Pt, bcc/fcc PdCu@Pt, and fcc/fcc Ru@Pt. We have identified distinct heteroepitaxial modes in these model systems, each mitigating the structural mismatch within a single particle: mixed coherent/semi-coherent growth in hcp/fcc Ru@Pt, coherent growth with strain sharing between core and shell in bcc/fcc PdCu@Pt, and oriented growth combined with twin proliferation in decahedral fcc/fcc Ru@Pt. The various semi-coherent growth modes in the hcp/fcc nanoparticle yield a 3D dislocation network at a scale below 10 nm, interconnected by Lomer–Cottrell, Hirth, and Shockley dislocations. The key heteroepitaxial mechanisms in these examined systems are quantitatively validated by interfacial energies derived from molecular statics simulations. We anticipate these insights will inform the targeted design of interfacial structures and enable precise strain engineering in core–shell nanomaterials.

motivation: Understanding how interfacial defects and strain relaxation accommodate structural mismatch in heteroepitaxial nanoparticles is crucial for engineering atomic arrangements.
method: Atomic-resolution electron tomography was used to determine 3D atomic structures of Pt-based core-shell nanoparticles (hcp/fcc Ru@Pt, bcc/fcc PdCu@Pt, fcc/fcc Ru@Pt), combined with molecular statics simulations.
result: Distinct heteroepitaxial modes were identified: mixed coherent/semi-coherent growth, coherent growth with strain sharing, and oriented growth with twin proliferation, including a 3D dislocation network below 10 nm.
conclusion: The insights can inform targeted design of interfacial structures and precise strain engineering in core-shell nanomaterials.
